title: What did Java 10 `var` add (local variable type inference), and what are its limitations (locals only, no null, readability trade-off)?
shortTitle: What did Java 10 var add, and what are its limitations?

s1_definition.profdef: `var` is a reserved type name introduced in Java 10 that enables local variable type inference. When you write `var x = expression;`, the compiler infers the static type of `x` from the type of the initializer and bakes that exact type into the bytecode. It is pure compile-time syntactic sugar — there is no runtime cost, no dynamic typing, and the variable is just as strongly typed as if you had written the type by hand. It is restricted to local variables with an initializer; it cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, or a bare declaration with no initializer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a teller at National Bank of India filling out a form. The old rule said she must write the full category name twice — "Savings Account Ledger Entry" in the left box, then "new Savings Account Ledger Entry" in the right box — even though the right box already makes the category obvious. `var` lets her write just "this entry equals a new Savings Account Ledger Entry," and the bank's system still records it under the exact same category, Savings Account Ledger Entry, nothing fuzzier. The category is fixed and strict; she simply did not have to write it twice. But she cannot write `var` on an empty box with nothing in it, because then the system would have no way to know the category.
s1_definition.oneliner: `var` lets the compiler infer a local variable's exact static type from its initializer; it is compile-time sugar, not dynamic typing, and works only on locals that are initialized.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `var` is a reserved type name introduced in Java 10 that enables local variable type inference. When you write `var x = expression;`, the compiler infers the static type of `x` from the type of the initializer and bakes that exact type into the bytecode. It is pure compile-time syntactic sugar — there is no runtime cost, no dynamic typing, and the variable is just as strongly typed as if you had written the type by hand. It is restricted to local variables with an initializer; it cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, or a bare declaration with no initializer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a teller at National Bank of India filling out a form. The old rule said she must write the full category name twice — "Savings Account Ledger Entry" in the left box, then "new Savings Account Ledger Entry" in the right box — even though the right box already makes the category obvious. `var` lets her write just "this entry equals a new Savings Account Ledger Entry," and the bank's system still records it under the exact same category, Savings Account Ledger Entry, nothing fuzzier. The category is fixed and strict; she simply did not have to write it twice. But she cannot write `var` on an empty box with nothing in it, because then the system would have no way to know the category.

**One line to remember:** `var` lets the compiler infer a local variable's exact static type from its initializer; it is compile-time sugar, not dynamic typing, and works only on locals that are initialized.

sections.s2_technical:
`var` reduces the boilerplate of repeating a type that the right-hand side already states. Writing `var accounts = new ArrayList<Account>();` is identical in every way to `ArrayList<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<Account>();` — the inferred type is `ArrayList<Account>`, and the bytecode is byte-for-byte the same. The key mental model: `var` is NOT like JavaScript's `var` or Python's dynamic variables. The type is fixed at compile time and can never change. If you do `var x = new BigDecimal("10");`, then `x = "hello";` is a compile error, because `x` is permanently a `BigDecimal`.

The inference always picks the type of the initializer expression. For `var fee = BigDecimal.ZERO;` the type is `BigDecimal`. For `var ids = List.of("SAV2001", "CUR3001");` the type is `List<String>`. One subtle point: `var` infers the most specific type, so `var list = new ArrayList<String>();` gives `ArrayList<String>`, not `List<String>`. If you need the interface type, you must write it explicitly.

Now the limitations, which interviewers love to probe. First, locals only: `var` is allowed for local variables, the index variable of a for-loop, and resources in try-with-resources, but not for fields, method parameters, method return types, or constructor parameters. Second, an initializer is mandatory: `var x;` does not compile because there is nothing to infer from. Third, you cannot initialize with `null` alone, as in `var x = null;`, because `null` has no definite type. Fourth, you cannot use `var` with array initializer shorthand, so `var arr = {1, 2, 3};` fails, though `var arr = new int[]{1,2,3};` works. Fifth, `var` cannot be used for a lambda or a method reference without a target type, because those need the compiler to already know the functional interface, so `var f = x -> x + 1;` fails.

A real trap is inference with the diamond operator and with primitives. `var count = 0;` infers `int`, and `var rate = 0.05;` infers `double`, which is usually fine but can surprise you if you expected `long` or `float`. With generics, `var m = new HashMap<String, BigDecimal>();` is a great use because it removes a long duplicated type, whereas `var result = service.process();` can hurt because the reader cannot tell what `process` returns without opening the method.

The readability trade-off is the senior point. `var` is not free — it hides the declared type at the call site. The community guideline, from the official style guidance, is to use `var` when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, such as a constructor call or a well-named factory, and to avoid it when the type would otherwise be informative, such as a primitive that matters for overflow or a method return whose type is not evident. Used well, it reduces noise in dense generic code; used carelessly, it forces readers to run the type in their head.

Note that `var` is not a keyword — it is a reserved type name. This means existing code that used `var` as a variable or method name still compiles, which was a deliberate backward-compatibility decision. You could even have a variable named `var` of type `var` in theory, though you never should.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The settlement team at National Bank of India had code full of painfully long generic declarations like `Map<String, List<TransactionRecord>> grouped = new HashMap<String, List<TransactionRecord>>();`. The type was written twice and dominated the line, burying the actual intent. This is exactly what `var` cleans up: `var grouped = new HashMap<String, List<TransactionRecord>>();` says the same thing once, and the inferred type is identical.

Problem 2 — A junior developer tried to write `var balance;` and later assign it, and separately `var amount = null;`, and both failed to compile. This is exactly the limitation that `var` needs an initializer with a definite type — the compiler cannot infer a type from nothing, and `null` has no type of its own.

Problem 3 — Another developer wrote `var total = account.computeInterest();` and the next reader could not tell whether total was a `BigDecimal`, a `double`, or a custom result object. This is the readability trade-off: `var` should be avoided when the initializer does not make the type obvious.

The mini-project is an interest and settlement summary routine. We will show good `var` uses where the type is obvious, show the inferred type is strict by demonstrating a reassignment that would fail, and illustrate the limitations in comments. We compute interest for Rajesh and group a few transactions for Priya.

The code contains: a `Transaction` class; an `InterestCalculator`; and a runnable demo showing good `var`, strict typing, and the limitation cases.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is Rajesh's balance Rs.1000000 at a 6 percent rate, plus three transactions, two for SAV2001 (Rs.50000 and Rs.25000) and one for CUR3001 (Rs.10000).

Step 1: `var rajeshBalance = new BigDecimal("1000000.00")`. The compiler looks at the initializer, sees a `BigDecimal`, and permanently types `rajeshBalance` as `BigDecimal`. At run time this variable holds Rs.1000000.

Step 2: `var transactions = new ArrayList<Transaction>()`. The inferred type is `ArrayList<Transaction>`. Three transactions are added; the data now lives inside the list on the heap.

Step 3: `calculator.computeInterest(rajeshBalance, rate)` multiplies Rs.1000000 by 0.06 and rounds to two decimals, producing Rs.60000.00. The result is stored in an explicitly typed `BigDecimal interest`, chosen on purpose so the reader sees the type.

Step 4: The enhanced for-loop declares `var txn`, inferred as `Transaction`. Each iteration reads one transaction.

Step 5: `grouped.merge(...)` accumulates amounts per account. SAV2001 becomes Rs.75000 (50000 plus 25000), CUR3001 becomes Rs.10000.

Step 6: The final grouped map is logged. At no point did `var` change behaviour — every inferred type is exactly what an explicit declaration would have produced.

```
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:10 PM com.bank.settle.VarDemo main
INFO: Rajesh interest on Rs.1000000.00 = Rs.60000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:10 PM com.bank.settle.VarDemo lambda$main$3
INFO: Account SAV2001 total Rs.75000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:10 PM com.bank.settle.VarDemo lambda$main$3
INFO: Account CUR3001 total Rs.10000.00
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — var Inference Rules ═══

  ┌─ Rules the compiler applies ──────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. Infer type from the initializer expression            │
  │  2. Pick the MOST SPECIFIC type (ArrayList, not List)     │
  │  3. Require an initializer (no bare `var x;`)              │
  │  4. Reject `null` alone (no definite type)                │
  │  5. Reject lambda/method-ref without target type          │
  │  6. Locals / for-index / try-with-resources ONLY          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Allowed vs Not Allowed ─────────────────────────────────

  [ALLOWED]                          [NOT ALLOWED]
   var x = new BigDecimal("10")       var f;                (no init)
   for (var t : list)                 var n = null;         (no type)
   try (var r = open())               var a = {1,2,3};      (array sugar)
   var m = new HashMap<K,V>()         field: var fee;       (not local)
                                      void m(var p)         (parameter)
                                      var foo() { }         (return type)

  ── Decision State: should I use var here? ──────────────────

  [initializer obvious?] ──yes──→ [USE var]  (less noise, same type)
         │
         no
         ▼
  [USE explicit type]  (reader needs the type to understand the code)

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. javac parses `var grouped = new HashMap<String,BigDecimal>()`
  2.   → infers HashMap<String,BigDecimal>, writes it to class file
  3. runtime: behaves exactly as an explicit HashMap<String,BigDecimal>
  4. merge() accumulates totals; no var involvement at runtime
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The var keyword, added in Java 10, gives local variable type inference. When I write var followed by an initializer, the compiler infers the exact static type from the right-hand side and bakes that type into the bytecode. The crucial point I always stress is that this is pure compile-time sugar and not dynamic typing. The variable is just as strongly typed as if I had written the type by hand, the bytecode is identical, and there is no runtime cost whatsoever. If I say var balance equals a BigDecimal, then balance is permanently a BigDecimal and assigning a string to it later is a compile error.

The limitations are where interviewers test depth, so I know them cold. var works only for local variables, the index of a for loop, and resources in try-with-resources. It cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, or constructor parameters. It always needs an initializer, so a bare var x does not compile, and it cannot be initialized with null alone because null has no definite type. It also cannot type a lambda or method reference by itself, because those need a target type the compiler must already know, and it does not work with the curly-brace array initializer shorthand.

In my banking code at National Bank of India, var genuinely cleaned up the settlement service, where we had declarations like a map of string to list of transaction record written twice on one line. Collapsing that to a single var declaration removed real noise while keeping the exact same strict type. But I am disciplined about the readability trade-off. I use var when the type is obvious from the initializer, such as a constructor call or a clearly named factory. I deliberately keep the explicit type when it is informative, for example when a method returns a value whose type is not evident at the call site, or when a primitive's exact type matters for overflow. The guideline I follow is simple: var should make code easier to read, so if hiding the type forces the next engineer to go hunting, I write the type out.
